posts.title: The Cards She Left Behind
posts.description: Some memories are tucked away in boxes. Others are tucked away in our hearts. My mother had a beautiful way of making people feel special. For every birthday, holiday, celebration, or special occasion, she would take the time to hand paint cards for the people she loved. They weren’t just cards. They were pieces of her. Each brushstroke, each word, each little detail carried her love. She could have easily bought a card from a store, but that wasn’t Mom. She wanted the people she loved to know that they were worth her time, her creativity, and her thoughtfulness. Mom passed away in December, 2022, with my son (her grandson) and my Dad at her side. And somehow, she still finds ways to speak to my heart. I still hear her words. I still carry her wisdom. I still think about the lessons she taught me, sometimes in the simplest moments. posts.title: Built In The Chrysalis
posts.description: There’s something about a monarch butterfly that makes you pause. Not because it’s loud or flashy, but because it’s proof that transformation doesn’t have to announce itself to be powerful. It starts as something small. A caterpillar. Grounded. Hungry. Consumed with the work of becoming, even if it doesn’t know what that means yet. No wings. No spotlight. Just quiet growth. Sound familiar? Most of us live in that phase longer than we expected. Doing the work. Carrying the weight. Wondering if all this effort is leading anywhere meaningful. It’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. But it’s necessary. Then comes the part we don’t talk about enough. The chrysalis. That in between space where everything falls apart before it comes together. Inside that tiny casing, the caterpillar doesn’t just grow wings. It completely breaks down. Its old form dissolves. It literally becomes unrecognizable before it becomes something new. posts.title: Why Your “Check Engine” Light is On (And It’s Not the Car)
posts.description: Remember the first car you owned? Mine was a beat-up hatchback that rattled if I went over 55. When the check engine light came on, I did what any self-respecting Gen Xer did: I ignored it until the car literally died in the middle of an intersection. We’re doing the same thing with our lives, folks. We’re driving on bald tires, ignoring the smoke under the hood, and wondering why we’re feeling burnt out and bitter. It’s time to pull over. We grew up as the “latchkey” generation. We learned early on that if we didn’t fix the sandwich or finish the homework, nobody else was going to do it for us. That self-reliance is our superpower, but it’s also our kryptonite. We’ve become so good at “sucking it up” that we’ve forgotten how to actually check in with ourselves.
